To explore patients' subjective experiences of traditional hospital services and residential alternatives to hospital, in-depth interviews were conducted with 40 carefully selected patients in residential alternative services who had previously experienced hospital in-patient stays. Eligible patients (aged 18 to 65) were identifi ed by staff and were interviewed in-depth by a single researcher for up to 2 h duration using a topic guide. The in-depth interviews were audiotaped and transcribed and analysed using thematic analysis. Initially four interviews were independently coded and an open coding session between four researchers was used to confer on and list themes. Findings and emerging themes were tested for validity through discussion – in both one-to-one and group meetings – by an interdisciplinary team comprising researchers with psychiatric, psychological and social work backgrounds, both with and without clinical experience and experience of using mental health services. Patients reported an overall preference for residential alternatives. These were identifi ed as treating patients with lower levels of disturbance, being safer, having more freedom and decreased coercion, and having less paternalistic staff compared with traditional in-patient services. However, patients identifi ed no substantial diff erence between their relationships with staff overall and the care provided between the two types of services. Which of the following can be considered as strength of this study?
options: Avoiding inter-rater variability by using single interviewer
Choosing patients with a shared experience of hospital in-patient stay
The use of an interdisciplinary approach to validate emerging themes
correctAnswer: The use of an interdisciplinary approach to validate emerging themes
explanation: The use of multiple coders for validating emerging themes has provided a mode of triangulation that increases the validity of the reported study.

stem: Kelly Y, Kelly J, Sacker A. Changes in bedtime schedules and behavioral diffi culties in 7-year-old children. Pediatrics. 2013 Oct 1:peds-2013. To investigate the causal links between disrupted sleep and behavioural problems in nonclinical populations, researchers utilised the data from 10,230 7-year-olds from the UK Millennium Cohort Study from births in the United Kingdom between September 2000 and January 2002. The bedtime data was collected at 3, 5, and 7 years with the question "On weekdays during term-time, does your child go to bed at a regular time?" (response categories were binarised to refer to regular vs. irregular bedtime), and behavioural diffi culties scores (Strengths and Diffi culties Questionnaire (SDQ) as rated by mothers and teachers at age 7. The analysis of relationship between bedtime hours and behavioural disturbances was adjusted for age and gender in the initial model (Model A) and for various other factors that could potentially mediate the results in a second model (Model B). These include birth order, family income, highest parental qualifi cation, mother's psychological distress, discipline strategies score, mother being often irritated with child, mother's parenting competence, breastfeeding, child skipping breakfast, child being helped with reading, math, writing, TV and computer hours per weekday, parental employment, parental view of amount of time with child, child attending breakfast club, any other child care, child being read to, TV time rules, overcrowding, child wetting bed, child's sleep being disturbed by wheezing and TV in bedroom. Children with nonregular bedtimes had more behavioural diffi culties. There was an incremental worsening in behavioural scores as exposure through early childhood to not having regular bedtimes increased: mother rated (nonregular any 1 age, ß = 0.53; nonregular any 2 ages, ß = 1.04; nonregular all 3 ages, ß = 2.10, P < .001) and teacher rated (ß = 0.22, ß = 0.73, ß = 1.85, P < .001). For children who changed from nonregular to regular bedtimes there were clear nontrivial, statistically signifi cant improvements in behavioural scores: A change between age 3 and 7 corresponded to a diff erence of ß = -0.63, and a change between age 5 and 7 corresponded to a diff erence of ß = -1.02). For children who changed from regular to nonregular bedtimes between ages 5 and 7 there was a statistically signifi cant worsening in scores, ß = 0.42. What type of study is this?
explanation: The exposure is irregular bedtime routine; the outcome is behavioural diffi culties. The authors utilised a dataset from a cohort in a retrospective fashion to identify exposed individuals and traced them forwards to see the rate of the outcome of interest. This is a retrospective cohort study. The authors could have done a nested case-control design, if theyfi rst determined the 'cases' and 'controls' by identifying all subjects with the categorical outcome of diffi cult behaviour, and then compared the rate of occurrence of irregular sleep patterns. As they did not employ this second approach, the best answer is 'Retrospective Cohort' design.

stem: Your patient with treatment resistant depression who is currently taking an SSRI medication, prints an article off the internet about a study of folate supplements given to patients with SSRI-resistant depression. A modifi ed summary of the article is given below. Method: 75 outpatients with SSRI-resistant major depressive disorder were enrolled in a 60-day study divided into two 30-day periods. Patients were randomly assigned, in a 2:3:3 ratio, to receive in a double-blind fashion l-methylfolate for 60 days (15 mg/day), placebo for 30 days followed by l-methylfolate (7.5 mg/day) for 30 days, or placebo for 60 days. In phase 1 (fi rst 30 days), patients were randomly assigned to drug or placebo, with more patients in the placebo arm. In the second phase, patients who did not respond to placebo in phase 1 were randomized to drug and placebo again. This latter group was pooled with patients from phase 1 for the analysis of outcome. SSRI dosages were kept constant throughout the study. Response according to the HAM-D (17 items) was defi ned as a reduction of ≥ 50% in HAM-D score during treatment (or afi nal score of ≤ 7). Results: Adding l-methylfolate 15.0 mg/day plus ongoing SSRI treatment produced a 32.3% response rate, compared to 14.6% for augmentation with placebo. Side eff ects in the two groups were comparable in type and frequency. There was no statistically signifi cant diff erence in the change in weight, supine and standing heart rate, or supine and standing diastolic and systolic blood pressure between the l-methylfolate and placebo groups in phase 1 or 2. From the given summary, calculate the NNT for the supplemental treatment:
explanation: Rate of response for placebo arm (CER) = 14.6%. Rate of response for folate arm (EER) = 32.3%. Diff erence (ARR or ABI) = 17.7%. NNT = 1/ARR = 100/17.7 = 5.65 rounded up as 6. So, NNT = 6

stem: A 42-year-old woman is a long standing user of skunk cannabis. She has recently stopped taking it and presents to A&E with irritability, agitation and impulsive aggression. Which of the following pharmacological option is most suitable?
explanation: The validity of a cannabis withdrawal syndrome is now well established. Agitation is a common feature associated with cannabis withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are commonly used for symptomatic relief during cannabis withdrawal, though there is currently no data to support this approach.

stem: Increased need for handling in babies is seen in withdrawal of which of the following drug;
explanation: Nicotine withdrawal syndromes: the severity depends on the nature of drugs and the frequency of use by the mother during pregnancy. Mild signs such asfi ne tremors and variations in tone; recent data indicates subtle neonatal behaviours, such as poor self-regulation and an increased need for handling. (Ref: Wang M. (2004) Perinatal drug abuse and neonatal withdrawal syndrome. Medscape e Medicine http://emedicine.medscape.com/article/978492-overview)

stem: John is a 79-year-old gentleman with insomnia. He is requesting to prescribe medication for his sleep problem. Which drug should be avoided in his case?
explanation: In older adults, with sleep onset problems, a short acting agent such as Lorazepam or Oxazepam may be eff ective. Long acting Benzodiazepines like Diazepam and Chlordiazepoxide are not recommended for insomnia in older adults. The commonly used non- Benzodiazepine agents include Zopiclone, Zolpidem and Zaleplon. They have been shown to be eff ective in short-term management of insomnia.

stem: Mr P is currently on Naltrexone. This drug can prevent relapses in the treatment of which of the following substance use disorders?
explanation: Naltrexone should be off ered for relapse prevention in moderately to severely dependent drinkers, in combination with psychosocial treatment. It should be prescribed for up to 6 months, or longer for those who perceive benefi t and wish to continue taking it. (NICE clinical guidelines Pg115, 2011)

stem: Mr Y has an alcohol dependence. He had his routine blood tests done recently. It showed raised AST and ALT levels. Which one among the following benzodiazepines could be used if required for his treatment?
explanation: RaIsed AST and ALT levels suggest possible hepatic impiarment. In terms of sedation, drugs like Lorazepam, Oxazepam and Temazepam are recommended for the treatments of patients with hepatic impairment. These drugs have short half life with no active metabolites. Use low doses with caution, as sedative drugs can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.

stem: Robert has a history of chronic alcoholism and now diagnosed with Korsakoff 's psychosis. Which of the following tests will NOT be impaired?
explanation: Patients with Korsakoff psychosis perform well on Digit span subtest of WAIS. But due to episodic memory loss, they lose scores on recall test in MMSE and AMT. In addition, a degree of frontal dysfunction results in a reduction in overall WAIS scores, which may recover over a period of time if the patient remains abstinent from alcohol. Interstigly, amnesic patients show elevated scores in several domains of MMPI, highlighting the frontal damage eff ects of alcohol abuse. In addition, MMPI also has a substance abuse scale in it. (Ref: http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3370157/ Also see Egger, et al (2002). Korsakoff 's syndrome on the MMPI-2 . Acta Neuropsychiatrica, 14, pp 231-236)

stem: A 17-year-old female with a BMI of 17 believes she is obese. She is always on a low calorie diet and walks excessively. Her menstrual cycles are regular. What is her probable diagnosis?
explanation: Atypical anorexia nervosa is the term used for those individuals in whom one or more of the key features of anorexia nervosa, such as amenorrhoea or signifi cant weight loss, is absent but who otherwise present a fairly typical clinical picture. (Ref: ICD10)

stem: Melatonin is considered to be an eff ective treatment for children with neurodevelopmental disorders. Which of the following signifi cantly increases on using melatonin?
explanation: Melatonin appears to shorten the time to fall asleep (reduces latency). It also improves total rapid-eye movement (REM) duration (reduces REM latency). The number of sleep interruptions reduce with melatonin use in children. De Leersnyder, H et al. Prolonged-release melatonin for children with neurodevelopmental disorders. Paediatric Neurology 2011; 45:23-26.

stem: A 4-year-old boy was brought in to the clinic, as his mother was concerned about his sleepwalking problem. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding sleepwalking?
options: It seems to run in families
Sleep walking is common in children
Injury may occur during sleep walking
Child usually wakes up during sleep walking
It typically occurs between the ages of 4 and 8
correctAnswer: Child usually wakes up during sleep walking
explanation: Sleepwalking can start at any age, but is more common in children. It's thought that at least 20% of children will sleepwalk at least once. Sleepwalking mostly happens in childhood, typically between the ages of 4 and 8.The exact cause of sleepwalking is unknown, but it seems to run in families. The child or the person usually has no recollection of the episode the following morning. Injury may occur like falling down the stairs etc. Eyes are usually wide open and talk is incoherent with communication usually impossible. If awakened during the episode, they are confused and disorientated.

stem: A 7-year-old boy presented with motor tics with facial grimacing for 1 year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The predominant manifestation in tic disorders is some form of tic. A tic is an involuntary, rapid, recurrent, non-rhythmic motor movement (usually involving circumscribed muscle groups), or vocal production, that is of suddent onset and serves no apparent purpose. The absence of vocal tics in this patient makes a diagnosis of Tourette's syndrome unlikely. The duration of at least a year makes chronic motor tics the most likely diagnosis.

stem: Choose the true statement among the following regarding ADHD
options: Co-morbid psychiatric illness is less common in ADHD children
Behaviour therapy should be tried after drug therapy
explanation: In mild to moderate cases of ADHD, thefi rst line treatments are usually behaviour therapy and education. Medication is indicated only in severe cases. Stimulant drugs ssuch as Methylphenidate and dexamfetamine are eff ective in around 70% of cases with around 95% having a clinically meaningful response to one drug or the other. Atomoxetine is a suitablefi rst line alternative to Methylphenidate, it is not a second line drug. It is a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor. It is not a controlled drug and a non stimulant. Co-morbid psychiatric illness is more common in ADHD children (Ref: Fundamentals of Clinical Psychopharmacology;126)

explanation: Imprinting of the same region on chromosome 15 has been implicated for 2 conditions- Angelman and Prader-Willi syndromes. It is the loss of the maternal contribution that is linked to Angelman syndrome and the loss of the paternal contribution that is linked to Prader-Willi syndrome.

stem: According to large follow-up studies the most important mediator of violence in patients with mental illness is
options: Recent discharge from a mental health unit
Presence of strangers in the immediate neighbourhood
explanation: Substance misuse is the most important risk factor for violence both in general and mentally disordered populations.

stem: Identify the true statement regarding pseudologia fantastica
options: Absence of speech without impairment of consciousness
An exaggerated sense of one's own importance
Episode of discrete amnesia related to alcohol intoxication
A form of delusional belief shared by 2 close people
explanation: Pseudologia fantastica is one of the more extreme forms of pathological lying. This is a matrix of facts andfi ction, mixed together in a way that makes the reality and fantasy almost indistinguishable. It is usually seen in forensic practice.

stem: The duty to warn the 3rd parties in case of imminent danger is illustrated by
explanation: Physicians and therapists in many jurisdictions have a duty to warn third parties of threatened danger arising from a patient's violent intentions. If the risk to third parties is so serious that it outweighs the patient's privacy interest then the appropriate person or authority should be informed without undue delay. (Tarasoff case)

stem: The highest risk factor for suicide in a prisoner is:
explanation: The suicide rate in prison more than doubled between 1982 and 1998, from 54 to 128 per 100 000 of the average annual prison population. Self-infl icted deaths currently represent about half of all deaths in prison and local prisons bear the highest brunt of prison suicides. Prison suicides have risen sharply in United Kingdom in recent years. Suicide is now nearly 8 times higher in the prison population than in the general population.The majority occurs within 6 months of imprisonment. The most common method is hanging. Life-sentence prisoners are over-represented. Alcohol and substance misuse is the most likely psychiatric problem.

explanation: There are various diff erences between male and female off enders. These include: women making more 'psychiatric' pleas than men, women receiving more psychiatric disposals than men and the victims of women's violent acts more likely to be family members.

stem: Which of the following is included in the criteria to assess one'sfi tness to plead? The person can
options: Speak to the police about the crime
Remember details of the alleged off
Understand the charges brought against them
correctAnswer: Understand the charges brought against them
explanation: The Fitness to Plead / Pritchard Criteria relates to the mental state of the defendant at the time of the trial. They include: ability to understand charges; ability to follow proceedings; ability to instruct counsel; ability to understand the diff erence between pleading guilty and not guilty; and the ability to challenge a juror. These factors are relevant at the time of the trial only. Amnesia for the off ense does not interfere with one'sfi tness to plead.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely symptom in a prisoner with Ganser's syndrome?
explanation: Ganser's syndrome is a rare dissociative disorder. The core features of Ganser's syndrome are approximate answers, clouding of consciousness, somatic conversion symptoms and hallucinations.

stem: Which of the following types of stalker is more likely to commit a homicide than the others listed?
explanation: A very low percentage of stalkers kill their victims; but a high percentage of those who have killed or attempted to kill women have stalked them beforehand. Predatory type of stalking is more commonly associated with serious violence; resentful stalkers are least likely to involve in serious violent off ences. http://bjp.rcpsych.org/content/176/3/206

stem: A 20 year old young man presented with fever, acute onset of confusion and memory impairment. CSF shows normal glucose concentration, increased proteins and lymphocytosis. The most likely diagnosis is;
explanation: HSE (Herpes simplex encephalitis) is the most common cause of limbic encephalitis. It is usually due to HSV-1. The clinical features include high fever, headaches, abrupt onset of confusion, change in personality and memory impairment, usually of acute onset. CSFfi ndings include pleocytosis (raised white cell count) and elevated proteins. Viral encephalomyelitis leads to a lymphocytosis with normal CSF/plasma glucose ratio.

stem: A 43 year old man with Schizoaff ective disorders is taking Risperidone and Citalopram. He develops tremor. What would be the next course of action?
explanation: Tremor is a possible side eff ect of both SSRIs like citalopram and antipsychotics like Risperidone. However risperidone is more likely to induce pseudoparkinsonian symptoms like tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia. Therefore, the next step is to reduce the dose of Risperidone (lowest possible dose of the antipsychotic medication should be used)

stem: A 52 year old woman on sodium valproate is complaining of severe abdominal pain. What is the most likely cause for this presentation?
explanation: Sodium valproate can cause serious complications such as acute pancreatitis and it has to be considered when choosing this medication for treating epilepsy and bipolar disorders in certain populations such as children and persons with intellectual disability. They present to the emergency department with an acute abdomen, vomiting and diarrhoea. Many side eff ects of sodium valproate are dose related and increase in frequency & severity when the plasma level is >100 mg/L.

stem: A patient presents to the A&E department with delirium, increased muscular rigidity, confusion and a high temperature. Which drugs must be avoided in this scenario?
explanation: The presentation is suggestive of Neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is important to avoid any agents thought to be causative especially antipsychotics.

stem: Clozapine must be used with caution in patients with which of the following disorders?
explanation: Being a potent anticholinergic agent, clozapine can result in anticholinergic toxicity. Caution is advised when using in the presence of narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, or other conditions where anticholinergic eff ects can produce signifi cant adverse reactions. https://www.pharma.us.novartis.com/product/pi/pdf/Clozaril.pdf

stem: ECT is contraindicated in patients with;
explanation: The usual contraindications to ECT are history of recent MI, history of recent cerebrovascular accident and any cause of increased intracranial pressure.With proper pre-ECT cardiac and pacemaker/defi brillator assessment, ECT can be safely and eff ectively administered to patients with an implanted cardiac device.

stem: In females, which of the following age group is associated with the highest risk of committing a homicide?
explanation: Over 40 per cent of female perpetrators of intimate partner homicide are aged between 30 and 39' - the average age being 35 years. (Brookman, F. Understanding Homicide. 2005. London, SAGE. p164)

stem: In your community clinic, you are reviewing a 45-year-old male who has bipolar aff ective disorder with a history of manic episodes. He is on lithium therapy only. He is fully compliant with his medication. In his last appointment, he complained of symptoms of hypomania, such as mood elation, irritability and reduced sleep. You increased the dose of his lithium to the maximum dose but this has had little eff ect. The patient is concerned about the persistence of his symptoms. What would be the most appropriate medication to add in order to prevent a relapse of mania?
explanation: For people with bipolar I disorder, for whom long-term therapy is clinically indicated, both combination therapy with lithium plus sodium valproate and lithium monotherapy are more likely to prevent relapse than is valproate monotherapy. This benefi t seems to be irrespective of baseline severity of illness and is maintained for up to 2 years. (BALANCE study, Lancet, 2010). The current NICE guidelines recommends adding antipsychotics such as olanzapine, risperidone or quetiapine to lithium when optimising lithium alone is insuffi cient in the treatment of acute mania; for maintenance phase, adding valproate is thefi rst recommendation when lithium is ineff ective . Antidepressants are not indicated in the treatment of hypomania or mania.

stem: Lucy has a history of paranoid psychosis and needed antipsychotic medication for possible relapse of her psychotic symptoms. She has a 4 month old baby and she is breastfeeding. Which of the following anti-psychotic medication should be avoided in this scenario?
explanation: According to the studies available, there is an increased risk of developing neutropenia and seizures in babies fed by mothers on Clozapine. A high breast milk clozapine level (2-3 times maternal plasma level) was also reported. Therefore it is advisable to avoid using clozapine in breastfeeding mothers.

stem: Lucy is keen to take depot medication for her psychosis. She tends to become depressed frequently and prefer to take a depot antipsychotic having antidepressant eff ect. The drug of choice is;
explanation: Flupenthixol decanoate (Depixol) has mood elevating eff ect. It is helpful in patients with psychosis and depressive symptoms. The dose range is 12.5-400 mg/week.

stem: Mark is a 21 year old man with a diagnosis of Paranoid Schizophrenia. He was treated on a course of Olanzapine for 8 weeks and then on Risperidone for 8 weeks with no improvement in his psychotic symptoms. What would be the next step?
options: Refer him to psychology for CBT
explanation: This is a case of treatment resistant Schizophrenia. NICE recommends that Clozapine should be used in treatment resistant schizophrenia where there has been a lack of satisfactory clinical improvement despite the sequential use of the recommended doses for 6 to 8 weeks of atleast 2 antipsychotics, atleast one of which should be an atypical. (Ref: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry:202)

stem: Miss P has quasipsychotic episodes with emotional disturbance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Quasipsychotic episodes with emotional disturbance (unpredictable aff ect) is seen in patients with borderline personality disorder

stem: Mrs X has a history of paranoid schizophrenia and started on an antipsychotic medication. She developed hypothyroidism on taking this drug. Identify the off ending drug?
explanation: Quetiapine is known to have adverse eff ects on thyroid function and can cause hypothyroidism. In clinical trials, patients treated with Quetiapine experienced a decrease in T4 levels and elevations in levels of TSH. It is now recommended that those on quetiapine should have thyroid function tests yearly although the risk of abnormality is very small (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines- Pg 46, 12th Edition)

stem: Professionals working in Recovery Teams concentrate primarily on which of the following aspects of a patient?
options: Assessment for mental and behavioural disorders
explanation: "Recovery" is associated with the loss of symptoms and the concept of cure, a personal process of learning how to live well with or without enduring symptoms or vulnerabilities. It is concerned with gaining hope, meaning, purpose, choice and control over patterns of living, as valued by the person themselves. (Ref: www.rcpsych.ac.uk)

stem: Robert has been diagnosed with a relapse of depressive illness. He took antidepressants in the past and had sexual side eff ects. In this episode, he would like to try the one with the lowest risk of sexual dysfunction. The drug of choice is;
explanation: Agomelatine and Bupropion have probably the lowest risk of sexual dysfunction. Bupropion is widely used in the USA as afi rst line antidepressant with minimal risk of sexual side eff ects and as antidote in patients with SSRI induced sexual dysfunction. (Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines; 11th edition: page 266)

stem: Severe personality disorder is a contraindication for the use of which of the following drugs used in addiction psychiatry?
explanation: Benzodiazepines are associated with increased impulsivity, disinhibition and increased levels of violence in people with Cluster B type personality disorders (disinhibition syndrome).

stem: The common biochemical changes identifi ed in patients with PTSD include
options: Raised basal cortisol level and elevated levels of corticotrophin releasing hormone
High secretion of cortisol and High secretion of catecholamines in urine
Reduced negative feedback suppression of the HPA axis by dexamethasone
Lower basal cortisol level and elevated levels of corticotrophin releasing hormone
Low secretion of cortisol and low secretion of catecholamines in urine
correctAnswer: Lower basal cortisol level and elevated levels of corticotrophin releasing hormone
explanation: The majority of research evidence and biochemical studies indicates people with PTSD have lower basal cortisol level, elevated levels of corticotrophin releasing hormone, and enhanced negative feedback suppression of the HPA axis by dexamethasone and high secretion of catecholamine in the urine.

stem: The connectivity between amygdala and which of the following brain structures is thought to be crucial for fear processing?
explanation: For regulation of emotions such as fear, the OFC acts as a central hub to integrate and modulate neural activation and control responses in conjunction with amygdala.

stem: The drug of choice for treatment of 'Defi cit syndrome' is;
explanation: The criteria for defi cit schizophrenia were designed to defi ne a group of patients with enduring and primary negative symptoms. Some second-generation antipsychotics have been shown to be generally superior tofi rst generation antipsychotics in the treatment of negative symptoms and data support the eff ectiveness of Amisulpride in primary negative symptoms.

stem: Thefi nal level in Goldberg & Huxley's pathway to psychiatric care model is
explanation: Goldberg & Huxley (1980) established the 'levels andfi lters' model to describe the wide range of severity of psychiatric disorders and pathways taken by patients to receive specialist care, from a patient's self-recognition in the community right through to thefi nal level: psychiatric inpatient admission.

stem: The most common cause of organic fugue reaction is
explanation: The most common cause of a fugue is a dissociative reaction. In the absence of dissociation, organic causes are likely. The most common organic cause is epilepsy temporal lobe). Other causes include brain tumours, head trauma and migraine.

stem: The most common presentation seen in women with post partum psychosis is:
explanation: Prominent aff ective symptoms (80%)-mania or depression with psychotic symptoms is the most common clinical presentation in women with post partum psychosis. Common features include lability of symptoms, insomnia, perplexity, bewilderment and disorientation: thoughts of suicide or infanticide (Ref: Oxford handbook of psychiatry- 420)

stem: The most common psychiatric presentation seen in patients with Multiple sclerosis is;
explanation: In people with Multiple Sclerosis, depression is common, with a point prevalence of 14-27% and lifetime prevalence of up to 50%. Suicide rates are 2-7.5 times higher than in the general population. Although anxiety also aff ects many people with Multiple Sclerosis, depression is the most common, with a point prevalence of 14-25% and lifetime prevalence of 35-37%.(Ref: The Maudsley prescribing guidelines; 11th edition: page 522)

stem: The most common symptom seen in patients with puerperal psychosis is;
explanation: In puerperal psychosis, delusions can frequently be paranoid in nature. Mums may believe that everyone (especially hospital staff and/or loved ones) is trying to harm her and/or her baby.

stem: Tomas's wife Clara develops manic symptoms following the delivery of theirfi rst baby. Tomas is anxious to know about the chance of relapse in future pregnancies?
explanation: The relapse rate of mood disorders in those who had a past history is around 50% when they are pregnant.

stem: What is the duration of treatment recommended for a 34 year old woman with bipolar aff ective disorder and a history frequent manic relapses with psychotic features?
explanation: Long term monotherapy or combination treatments in bipolar disorder should be continued for at least 2 years after an episode of bipolar disorder or up to 5 years if the person has risk factors for relapse (NICE CG38. Note that this recommendation is not backed by robust evidence, but has consensus support)

stem: What percentage of patients contacted the general practitioner within 1 month before attempting suicide?
explanation: According to the suicide staistics in England and Wales, 66% of patients contacted the general practitioner in the last four weeks before attempting suicide. In terms of older patients, it is 70%, who visited their primary care physician in the last 4 weeks before attempting suidice.

Primary appraisal is a person's judgment about the signifi cance of an event as stressful, positive, controllable, challenging or irrelevant. Facing a stressor, the second appraisal follows, which is an assessment of people's coping resources and options. Secondary appraisals address what one can do about the situation. Actual coping eff orts aimed at regulation of the problem give rise to outcomes of the coping process. The Transactional Model of Stress and Coping is a framework for evaluating how one copes with stressful events.

stem: Prevention & types Identify one correct option for each of the following preventive measures in schizophrenia Urban living for schizophrenia Identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state Cannabis and psychosis Environmental adjustments and aids in learning disabled adult. Choose... Choose... Choose... Choose...
correctAnswer: Urban living for schizophrenia → Universal prevention, Identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state → Indicated prevention, Cannabis and psychosis → Selective prevention, Environmental adjustments and aids in learning disabled adult. → Tertiary prevention
explanation: Universal prevention/interventions are directed to a general population group. For schizophrenia, some epidemiological factors such as urban living, poor social capital including low social cohesion, exclusion and discrimination, low socioeconomic status are so widespread that their targeting can be considered a universal intervention. Indicated interventions target high-risk individuals with minimal but detectable signs or symptoms foreshadowing mental disorder, but who do not meet diagnostic levels e.g identifi cation of a preschizophrenic state/prodrome of schizophrenia. Selective interventions are targeted to individuals or subgroups whose risk of developing disorder is signifi cantly higher than average. Perinatal complications and cannabis use have stimulated interest as a putative risk factors for schizophrenia. Both selective and indicated approaches are secondary prevention methods. Tertiary prevention helps an individual to attain his or her full developmental potential through rehabilitation, which includes education, support, environmental adjustments and aids.

3. Which ONE method is most useful to assess publication bias? Explanation: When reviewing the literature published in journals for a meta-analysis, it is important to note that papers with signifi cant positive results are more likely to be published [publication bias], especially in (1) English journals [some call this as the Tower of Babel bias] (2) indexed in more popular databases [database bias] and 930 cited more often than not [citation bias]. Hence it is important to search widely and include non-English journals while locating the papers. Statistical heterogeneity is said to exist if the point estimates of individual studies were variable in magnitude and if this variation between them is more than expected when taking samples from the same population. This variation can occur for a variety of reasons. If statistical heterogeneity is absent, afi xed eff ects meta-analysis should be suffi cient to estimate pooled eff ect size. If it exists, then a random eff ect analysis is preferred. Random eff ects approach tends to produce a wider confi dence interval for the pooled eff ect, thus refl ecting the uncertainity associated with the heterogeneity noted in the meta-analysis. A commonly employed statistical test for inferring the presence of heterogeneity is Cochran's Q (Chi-square) test which tests the null hypothesis that homogeneity exists between the sample estimates of the population parameter. Cochran's Q test lacks accuracy and is often accompanied by the use of Higgins I2 statistic that gives the percentage of variation between the sample estimates as a result of heterogeneity. I2 ranges from 0% to 100%, with 50% used as arbitrary cut-off above

which one must be concerned about statistical heterogeneity. (Adapted from Sedgwick, 2012: BMJ;344:e3971) Correct Answer is : 1. Considering papers not published in English, Using a wider literature search 2. Chi-square test, Random eff ect analysis 3. Funnel plot
